title: BAR U3·W2 — Capital Budgeting & Investment Decisions (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — should MBG buy the crane?

When Meridian Building Group weighs a $400,000 tower crane against years of rental, it is making a capital-budgeting decision — committing cash now for returns spread over years. BAR tests the techniques that rank such investments: net present value, internal rate of return, payback, and the profitability index, all resting on the time value of money and the cost of capital (WACC) from BAR Unit 2. This week builds the toolkit for deciding which long-term investments create value.

Relevant cash flows

Capital budgeting analyzes incremental, after-tax cash flows, not accounting income. Only future cash flows that differ between accepting and rejecting matter: the initial outlay, the operating cash inflows, the depreciation tax shield (depreciation is non-cash but reduces taxes), changes in working capital, and any salvage value. Sunk costs (already spent) and allocated overhead that will not change are excluded. Getting the cash flows right — incremental and after tax — is the foundation; the discounting techniques are only as good as the flows fed into them.

Net present value

Net present value (NPV) discounts all expected cash flows to the present at the firm's required rate of return (typically WACC) and subtracts the initial investment. The rule: accept if NPV is positive (the project earns more than the cost of capital and creates value); reject if negative. Worked example: a project costs $100,000 and returns $30,000 per year for five years; at a 10% discount rate the annuity factor is about 3.7908, so the inflows are worth $113,724 and NPV = $13,724 — positive, so accept. NPV is the theoretically preferred method because it measures value created in dollars and uses a realistic reinvestment assumption.

Internal rate of return

The internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero — the project's own expected return. The rule: accept if IRR exceeds the hurdle rate (the cost of capital). IRR is intuitive because it is expressed as a percentage, but it has drawbacks: it assumes cash flows are reinvested at the IRR (often unrealistic), can produce multiple IRRs with unconventional cash flows, and can conflict with NPV when ranking mutually exclusive projects of different size or timing. When NPV and IRR disagree on mutually exclusive projects, NPV governs.

Payback and discounted payback

The payback period is the time required to recover the initial investment from cash inflows — a $100,000 project returning $25,000 a year pays back in four years. It is simple and emphasizes liquidity and risk, but it ignores the time value of money and any cash flows after payback. The discounted payback period fixes the first flaw by using discounted cash flows, but still ignores post-payback flows. Payback is best as a screening or risk filter, not the primary accept/reject criterion.

Profitability index and accounting rate of return

The profitability index (PI) divides the present value of inflows by the initial investment; a PI greater than 1 means a positive NPV, so accept. PI is useful for ranking projects when capital is rationed, because it measures value created per dollar invested. The accounting rate of return (ARR) divides average accounting income by the investment — but because it uses accrual income and ignores the time value of money, it is the weakest method and is tested mainly as a contrast to the discounted techniques.

Comparing the methods

Each method answers a slightly different question. NPV gives value created in dollars (the best single measure); IRR gives a return percentage (intuitive but flawed for ranking); PI gives value per dollar (best under capital rationing); payback gives a liquidity/risk read. The discount rate matters enormously — a higher required return lowers every present value and can flip a positive NPV negative — which is why the WACC estimate from BAR Unit 2 is so consequential. For independent projects NPV and IRR agree; the conflicts arise only among mutually exclusive ones.

Risk and sensitivity

Because the inputs are forecasts, the analysis must test uncertainty. Sensitivity analysis changes one variable at a time (the discount rate, the cash-flow estimate) to see how the decision shifts; scenario analysis models coherent best/base/worst cases; and a higher risk-adjusted discount rate can be applied to riskier projects. For MBG, recognizing that a crane's value hinges on assumed utilization — and stress-testing that assumption — is as important as the point-estimate NPV. A single number hides the risk that sensitivity analysis reveals.

The time value of money toolkit

Every discounting technique rests on the time value of money: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later because it can be invested. The building blocks are the present value of $1 (discount a single future amount), the present value of an annuity (discount a stream of equal payments — the factor used in the NPV example), and their future-value counterparts. The discount rate reflects the required return, and compounding frequency matters — more frequent compounding raises the effective rate. Mastering which factor applies to which cash-flow pattern is the mechanical core of every capital-budgeting and valuation computation across BAR.

Capital rationing and mutually exclusive projects

Real firms face limited capital, so they must rank projects, not just accept every positive-NPV one. Under capital rationing, the profitability index helps select the combination of projects that maximizes total NPV per dollar of the constrained budget. Mutually exclusive projects (only one can be chosen — buy the crane or the larger one) are ranked by NPV, accepting the highest. Unequal lives are compared with techniques such as the equivalent annual annuity. The recurring lesson is that the accept/reject rule for an independent project differs from the ranking needed when resources or choices are constrained.

Real options in capital budgeting

Static NPV can understate a project's value by ignoring managerial flexibility. Real options — the option to expand a successful project, abandon a failing one, or defer investment until uncertainty resolves — carry value that traditional NPV misses. Recognizing that MBG could scale up crane use if its project pipeline grows, or sell the asset if work dries up, adds option value to the base analysis. The concept reminds analysts that a single discounted number is a starting point, not the whole decision.

CMA bridge

CMA months 8 and 11 built MBG's capital-budgeting and cost-of-capital models; BAR tests them at exam depth and ties them to the WACC and valuation work from BAR Unit 2. The equipment-versus-rent decision the CFO models every season is exactly the NPV/IRR analysis that decides whether a long-term investment creates value.

Practice and recap

  1. Use incremental, after-tax cash flows (include depreciation tax shield and working capital; exclude sunk costs).
  2. Apply NPV (accept if > 0; discount at WACC) and IRR (accept if > hurdle rate); when they conflict on mutually exclusive projects, NPV governs.
  3. Compute payback (ignores TVM and post-payback flows), discounted payback, and the profitability index (PI > 1 accept; ranks under capital rationing).
  4. Test risk with sensitivity and scenario analysis and a risk-adjusted discount rate.

Recap: capital budgeting discounts incremental after-tax cash flows; NPV (accept if positive — a $100,000 project returning $30,000 for five years at 10% has a $13,724 NPV) is the preferred measure of dollar value created, IRR (accept if above the hurdle) is an intuitive percentage that can conflict with NPV on mutually exclusive projects (where NPV governs), payback and discounted payback gauge liquidity but ignore later flows, and the profitability index (>1) ranks projects per dollar under capital rationing — all stress-tested with sensitivity and scenario analysis.

questions.q: A project should be accepted under the NPV rule when:
questions.explain: A positive NPV means the project earns more than the cost of capital and creates value.

questions.q: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which:
questions.explain: IRR is the rate that makes NPV = 0; accept if it exceeds the hurdle rate.

choices: Ignores the time value of money and post-payback cash flows

questions.q: The profitability index is most useful for:
choices: Ranking projects when capital is rationed
questions.explain: PI measures value per dollar invested, ideal for ranking under capital rationing; PI > 1 means accept.

questions.q: When NPV and IRR conflict for mutually exclusive projects, the decision should follow:
questions.explain: NPV uses a more realistic reinvestment assumption and measures dollar value, so it governs.

questions.q: Which is a relevant cash flow in capital budgeting?
questions.explain: Depreciation is non-cash but reduces taxes (a real cash effect); sunk costs and unchanged allocations are irrelevant.
